content: CD29, also referred to as integrin beta-1, is a protein encoded by the ITGB1 gene in humans. It functions as a subunit of integrins and is associated with very late antigen receptors. CD29 combines with the alpha-3 subunit to form the α3β1 complex, which interacts with molecules such as netrin-1 and reelin. In cardiac and skeletal muscle, a specific isoform known as integrin beta-1D is expressed. This isoform is localized to costameres, where it plays a critical role in the lateral transmission of force from the Z-discs to the extracellular matrix. Abnormal levels of integrin beta-1D have been observed in conditions such as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and polyneuropathy. Integrin beta-1 exists in multiple isoforms due to alternative splicing. Six alternatively spliced variants have been identified, encoding five proteins with different C-terminal regions. Integrin receptors are heterodimers, and more than 20 different heterodimeric integrin receptors have been described. All integrins, including alpha and beta forms, possess large extracellular domains and short intracellular domains. The cytoplasmic domain of integrin beta-1 binds to the actin cytoskeleton. Integrin beta-1 is the most abundant beta-integrin and associates with at least 10 different integrin-alpha subunits. Members of the integrin family are membrane receptors involved in cell adhesion and recognition processes, including embryogenesis, hemostasis, tissue repair, immune responses, and the metastatic spread of tumor cells. Integrins link the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix and mediate bidirectional signaling between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasmic domains. Beta-integrins are primarily responsible for targeting integrin dimers to specific subcellular locations, such as focal adhesions in adhesive cells. Mutations in integrin beta-1 result in the loss of its ability to localize to focal adhesion sites. Three novel isoforms of integrin beta-1 have been identified: beta-1B, beta-1C, and beta-1D. The beta-1B isoform is transcribed when the proximal 26 amino acids of the cytoplasmic domain in exon 6 are retained, followed by a 12-amino acid sequence from an adjacent intronic region. This isoform acts as a dominant negative, inhibiting cell adhesion. The beta-1C isoform contains an additional 48 amino acids appended to the 26 amino acids in the cytoplasmic domain and has an inhibitory effect on DNA synthesis during the G1 phase of the cell cycle. The beta-1D isoform is specific to striated muscle and replaces the canonical beta-1A isoform in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. It is produced through splicing into a novel exon between exons 6 and 7. The cytoplasmic domain of beta-1D replaces the distal 21 amino acids of beta-1A with an alternative 24-amino acid sequence, 13 of which are unique. This isoform is developmentally regulated during myofibrillogenesis, appearing immediately after myoblast fusion in C2C12 cells and increasing in levels throughout myofibrillar differentiation. Beta-1D integrin is specifically localized to costameres and intercalated discs in cardiac muscle, as well as costameres, myotendinous junctions, and neuromuscular junctions in skeletal muscle. It functions similarly to other integrins, as clustering of beta-1D integrins on the surface of CHO cells induces tyrosine phosphorylation of pp125FAK and activates mitogen-activated protein kinase. In patients with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2C, beta-1D integrin levels are significantly reduced in skeletal muscle biopsies, along with reductions in alpha-7B integrin and filamin-2. Similarly, in patients with sensory-motor polyneuropathy, levels of integrin alpha-7B, beta-1D, and agrin are markedly reduced, often to undetectable levels, corresponding with lower mRNA levels. CD29 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including ACTN1, CD46, CD9, FHL2, filamin, FLNB, CD81, GNB2L1, ITGB1BP1, LGALS8, MAP4K4, NME1, PKC alpha, TLN1, TSPAN4, and YWHAB.
